title: The good of all beings
hook: twice the Gita describes people near the goal as delighting in the good of all beings
carry: delight in the good of all beings

segments.voice: Yesterday closed our re-reading of karma with the lotus leaf: in the water all day, and offer every act to god; let the fruit go.

Sarvabhutahite ratah. A short Sanskrit phrase that turns up twice in the Gita, both times describing people who've come close to the goal. It means delighting in the good of all beings. Over six days, we'll sketch a year of service. Today, the reason under the whole thing.
screen: `TWICE IN THE GITA.` → `DELIGHTING IN THE GOOD OF ALL BEINGS.` → `SIX DAYS: A YEAR OF SERVICE.`

segments.voice: First, in paraphrase: near the end of chapter five, Krishna describes the sages who reach the peace of Brahman: their faults worn away, their doubts cut through, their selves held steady, delighting in the good of all beings. Then, in chapter twelve, Arjuna asks which worshipers know yoga better: those who love God with a form, or those who seek the imperishable, beyond form? Krishna answers that those who fix their minds on him are the most devoted. But of the second group he says: with the senses held in, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the good of all beings, they too come to me. The phrase sits not in a chapter on charity, not in a list of rules, but inside portraits of people near the end of the path. On this reading, care for others isn't only a road toward the goal. It's one of the marks of having come close to it. That gives seva, a word Hindus use for service, a particular root. Not service as an extra on a free weekend but as something a settled heart is glad to do. And look at the word all. Not all who agree with me, not all in my family or my town. All beings. Hindu homes have an old way of practicing that word. The law books list five daily offerings a householder makes, and one of them is to the beings: a little food set out for birds, animals, whatever lives nearby. It's why some grandmothers put out rice for the birds, or the first roti for a cow, before the family eats. A temple kitchen feeding whoever walks in is the same idea, bigger. So a year of service can start before any calendar: whose good would you be glad to see, and how far past your own people can that circle reach?
screen: `CHAPTER FIVE: THE SAGES NEAR THE GOAL.` · `CHAPTER TWELVE: THE SAME PHRASE.` · `CARE AS A MARK OF COMING CLOSE.` · `FOOD FOR THE BIRDS BEFORE BREAKFAST.` · then, large: `ALL BEINGS, NOT SOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose good you'd be glad to see today, then let the circle open one ring at a time, a neighbor, a coworker, a stranger in another city, an animal, a tree on your street, and notice where gladness gets harder, marking that place without pushing past it. If you pray, you can hold the whole circle before the one you pray to.
Sarvabhutahite ratah. Delighting in the good of all beings, a phrase from the Gita, said of those near the path's end.
Your line: delight in the good of all beings. Tomorrow, which service is yours. See you then.

howItsDone: Seva, selfless service, takes forms such as cooking and serving food at temples, caring for elders and guests, and cleaning shared spaces, and many Hindu homes keep the old daily offering to the beings: a little food set out for birds or animals before the family eats.
